senses: to glisten with a feature, usually with a colour
to burn, be strongly affected with an emotion (not always specified; when it is, most often in the ablative, but also with ad or in)
to be ardently or fervently in love, to burn with (especially romantic) desire
la:verb:ardeo.html:
ardĕo, rsi, rsum, 2,
v. n. (perf. subj. ARDVERINT, Inscr. Fratr. Arval., of the time of the emperor Alexander Severus, in ) [cf. Sanscr. ghar = to shine. Sonne foll. by Curt.], to take fire, to kindle; hence,
Lit., to be on fire, to burn, blaze (syn.: ardesco, exardeo, flagro, incendor, uror): Nam multis succensa locis ardent sola terrae,for the soil is on fire in different places,: tecta ardentia,: Ultimus ardebit, quem etc., i. e. His home will burn last, whom etc., : ardente domo,: radii ardentes,: circumstant cum ardentibus taedis, Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 51 Vahl.): caput arsisse Servio Tullio dormienti,: vis ardens fulminis,: Praeneste ardentes lapides caelo decidisse,: rogum parari Vidit et arsuros supremis ignibus artus,; ; : arsurae comae,: videbat quod rubus arderet,; ; .—
Trop.
Of the eyes, to flash, glow, sparkle, shine (syn.: fulgeo, inardesco, mico): ardent oculi,; ; ; cf.: oculi ejus (erant) ut lampas ardens,.—
Poet., transf. to color, to sparkle, glisten, glitter, dazzle: Tyrio ardebat murice laena,: campi armis sublimibus ardent,. —
In gen., of any passionate emotion

or excitement, to burn, glow, be inflamed, usu. with abl. (dolore, irā, studio, invidiā, etc.), but often without an abl.; to be strongly affected, esp. with love; to be inflamed, burn, glow, to blaze, be on fire, be consumed, etc. (syn.: ardesco, exardeo, furo).

With abl.: quippe patentia cum totiens ardentia morbis Lumina versarent oculorum, expertia somno,they rolled around the open eyeballs glowing with heat,: In fluvios partim gelidos ardentia morbo Membra dabant,their limbs burning with the heat of fever,: ardere flagitio,: amore,. 1, 27; : iracundiā,: curā,: dolore et irā,: cupiditate,: studio et amore,: desiderio,; : podagrae doloribus,to be tormented with,: furore, et saep.: cum arderet Syria bello,; ; al.—
Without an abl.: ipse ardere videris, (incensus esse, B. and K.); cf. : omnium animi ad ulciscendum ardebant,were fired, eager,: Ardet,: ultro implacabilis ardet,: ardet in arma,; so, in caedem,.—Poet. with inf. as object (cf. infra), to desire ardently to do a thing: ruere ardet utroque,: Ardet abire fugā dulcīsque relinquere terras,; ; .—Esp., to burn with love (syn. uror): ex aequo captis ardebant mentibus ambo,: deus arsit in illā, (cf.: laborantes in uno Penelopen vitreamque Circen,): arsit Virgine raptā,; cf. ; and with acc. of the object loved (as supra, in constr. with the inf.): formosum pastor Corydon ardebat Alexin, Corydon had a burning passion for, etc., : comptos arsit adulteri Crines,: delphini pueros miris et humanis modis arserunt,; cf. Arusian. Mess. p. 209 Lind. !*? * Pass. arsus, roasted, .—ardens, entis, P. a., prop. on fire, burning; hence, glowing, fiery, ardent, hot, etc., lit. and trop.
Lit.: sol ardentissimus, Tubero ap. : ardentissimum tempus,: Austri ardentes,: quinta (zona) est ardentior illis,hotter,: ardens Africa,.—
Trop.
Of the eyes: oculi,glowing,.—
Of color: ardentissimus color,: apes ardentes auro,glowing, glittering as with gold,; so .—
Of wounds, burning, smarting: ardenti morsu premere dolorem,with burning bite,.—
Of wine, strong, fiery: ardentis Falerni Pocula,; cf. .—
Of passion or strong feeling, burning, glowing, eager, impatient, ardent: avaritia ardens,: mortem ardentiore studio petere,: ardentes in eum litteras ad me misit,: ardentissimus dux,; : ardentissimus amor,, Reg. 11, 2: studia,: Nonne cor nostrum ardens erat in nobis,: furor,: miserere ardentis (sc. amore),.—Poet. with gen.: ardens caedis,.—In Cic. freq. of passionate, excited discourse: nec umquam is qui audiret, incenderetur, nisi ardens ad eum perveniret oratio,: verbum, (cf. ): nisi ipse (orator) inflammatus ad eam (mentem) et ardens accesserit,: orator gravis, acer, ardens,— Adv.ardenter, only trop., in a burning, fiery, eager, passionate manner, ardently, eagerly, passionately: ardenter aliquid cupere,; .— Comp.: ardentius sitire,to have a more burning thirst,: ardentius diligere,, : ardentius amare,.—Sup.: ardentissime diligere,; .

senses: the object of ardent affection, love, flame
la:noun:ardor.html:
ardor, ōris, m.
ardeo
,
a flame, fire, heat, burning heat, lit. and trop.
Lit.: solis ardor,: exortus est sol cum ardore,: ignium,: ignis, Pet. 3, 12: flammarum,: flammaï,: visas ab occidente faces ardoremque caeli,: ardor caelestis, qui aether vel caelum nominatur,: ardore deflagrare,: ardores corporum in morbis,: Visitabo vos in egestate et ardore,with burning fever,—
Trop.
Of the flashing fire of the eyes, brightness, brilliancy: fervescit et ex oculis micat acribus ardor,and fire gleams forth from the keen eyes,: ille imperatorius ardor oculorum,, and .—Of the external appearance in gen.: in te ardor voltuum atque motuum,: oris,animation,.—
Of the passions or feelings, heat, ardor, glow, impatience, eagerness, ardent desire: Sive voluptas est sive est contrarius ardor, i. e. dolor,some tormenting pain,: cupiditatum ardore restincto,: ardor mentis ad gloriam,: quem ardorem studii censetis fuisse in Archimede, qui etc.,: ardor animi non semper adest, isque cum consedit,: vultus ardore animi micans,: ardorem compescere,; . —Transf. from the combatants to the weapons: tantus fuit ardor armorum,: Ardorem cupiens dissimulare meum,glowing love,; so .— With obj. gen.: at te ejusdem virginis ardor Perdiderat,; ; —And meton., the object of ardent affection, love, flame: tu primus et ultimus illi Ardor eris,.

la:verb:ardesco.html:
ardesco, arsi, 3,
v. inch. [ardeo], to takefire, to kindle, to be inflamed (mostly poet. or in post-Aug. prose; not in Cic.; while exardesco is very freq.), lit. and trop.
Lit.: ut omnia motu Percalefacta vides ardescere,: ardescunt caelestia templa,: ne longus ardesceret axis,; .—
Trop., to gleam, glitter.
Of rays of light: fulmineis ardescunt ignibus undae,.—
Of the gleaming of a sword: pugionem in mucronem ardescere jussit,.—
Most freq. of the passions, to be inflamed, become more intense, increase in violence: ardescere dirā cuppedine,; so : in iras, (cf. : exarsit in iras, and : accensus in iram): in nuptias incestas,: ardescit tuendo,: stimulo ardescit,: quibus haec rabies auctoribus arsit,.—So, absol.: fremitus ardescit equorum,: ardescente pugnā,: in labiis ejus ignis ardescit, * .

senses: hard to reach, difficult, laborious, arduous
la:adj:arduus.html:
arduus, a, um, adj.
akin to ΑΡΔΩ, ἄρσω = to water, to cherish; ἀλδαίνω = to make grow; ἀλδήεις = growing; alo, altus, q. v.; 1. ad-oleo, ad-olesco; related to arbor, arbutus as ἐρυθρός, Germ. roth, Engl. red, is related to ruber; Ardea was perh. so called from its lofty situation; cf. Arduenna
,
high, elevated, lofty, steep (syn.: altus, celsus, sublimis).
Lit.: Pergama ardua, Enn. ap. : aether,: sidera,: cedrus,: cervix equi,: et campo sese arduus infert (Turnus),.—Also in prose in Gell.: supercilia,i. e. proudly elevated,: confragosus atque arduus clivis,steep,: ascensus,: arduus ac difficilis ascensus,: ardua et aspera et confragosa via,. 3: via alta atque ardua, Enn. ap. : mons,: Tmolus, al.—Hence, subst.: arduum, i, n., asteep place, a steep: Ardua dum metuunt, amittunt vera viaï,: in ardua montis Ite,: ardua terrarum,: per arduum scandere,: in arduo,: in arduis ponet nidum suum,: ardua Alpium,: castellorum,: ingressi sunt ardua,. —
Trop.
That is difficult to reach or attain, difficult, laborious, hard, arduous: magnum opus omnino et arduum conamur,: rerum arduarum ac difficilium perpessio,; so : id arduum factu erat,; : victoria,: virtus,: nil mortalibus arduum est,.—Subst.: nec fuit in arduo societas,.—
Troublesome, unpleasant: in primis arduum videtur res gestas scribere,, upon which Gellius remarks: Arduum Sallustius non pro difficili tantum, sed pro eo quoque ponit, quod Graeci χαλεπὸν appellant: quod est cum difficile tum molestum quoque et incommodum et intractabile,: quam arduum onus,.—
Of fortune, difficult, adverse, inauspicious: aequam memento rebus in arduis Servare mentem,in adversity,.!*? Comp. arduior: iter longius arduiusque erat, Cato ap. P.—Sup. arduissimus: asperrimo atque arduissimo aditu, Cato ap. P.; cf.: assiduus, egregius, industrius, perpetuus, and Rudd. I. p. 180, n. 58.—Adv. not used.
